% ABSTRACT — M5 writes
% ====================================================================
\begin{abstract}
Hydrate formation in offshore well service lines can cause costly shutdowns
and safety hazards if not detected early. This study compares three models
--- XGBoost (feature-engineered baseline), a Temporal Convolutional Network
(TCN), and a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) --- for early warning of hydrate
events using Petrobras's 3W Dataset~2.0.0 (Event~9). All three models are
evaluated at a matched false-alarm budget of one alarm per 100 operating
hours, with lead time (time from first alarm to annotated transient onset)
as the headline metric. Each model is trained under two conditions:
real-only and real-plus-simulated data. We employ grouped cross-validation
with well-level splits to prevent data leakage. Our results demonstrate that
\placeholder{M5: fill after S3 FREEZE — e.g. TCN under real-plus-simulated data achieved the best median lead time of X minutes and Y\% event recall}.

Reproduction: all code, data processing, and evaluation are available at
\url{https://github.com/AMammedova/team-hydrate3w}.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
hydrate formation, early warning, time series classification,
temporal convolutional network, gated recurrent unit, 3W dataset
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% ====================================================================
% I. INTRODUCTION — M1 writes
% ====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

% Written by M1. Every measured number quoted here is reproduced in
% Section~\ref{sec:dataset} with its source; none is hand-typed.

Hydrate formation in offshore well service lines is a slow-onset failure
mode. Gas hydrates crystallise inside flowlines under the combination of
pressure, temperature and water/gas content that offshore production
routinely produces, and a fully formed blockage can shut a well in for days.
The process is not instantaneous: it passes through a detectable transient
phase before the blockage establishes, which is what makes early warning a
meaningful goal rather than a post-hoc diagnosis. If a model recognises the
transient signature in the multivariate sensor stream early enough, an
operator gains lead time to intervene --- chemical injection, pigging, or a
rate change --- before the line is lost.

This paper builds and evaluates an early-warning classifier for hydrate
formation using Petrobras's 3W Dataset~2.0.0, event~9 (``Hydrate in
Production Line''), the largest public labelled collection of real and
simulated offshore well instrumentation for this class of problem. We frame
the task as three-class classification --- Normal, Transient, Established
--- over a sliding window of multivariate sensor readings, and we evaluate
every model at a \emph{matched} false-alarm budget of one alarm per 100
operating hours, so that lead time and false-alarm rate are comparable
across architectures rather than each being reported at its own convenient
operating point.

The dataset makes the problem harder than a window-classification framing
suggests, in two ways that shape every design decision in this paper. First,
the positive class is genuinely rare: of the 57 real event-9 instances, only
14 ever reach a transient phase and only 3 ever reach established blockage.
The project statement defines lead time against blockage onset; on a
well-grouped cross-validation that quantity is undefined in most test folds,
so we measure lead time against the annotated \emph{transient} onset and
report the blockage-referenced figure only as a secondary quantity with its
$n=3$ stated (Sections~\ref{sec:dataset} and~\ref{sec:method_eval}). Second,
the 15 wells that contribute event-9 recordings and the 9 wells that
contribute Normal-operation recordings are disjoint, so well identity alone
predicts the label. A model that shortcuts to ``which well is this'' can look
strong under a naive evaluation and fail on the next well; per-instance
normalisation and well-grouped splits are what close that shortcut.

The required result is a head-to-head comparison of a feature-engineered
gradient-boosted baseline (XGBoost) against two deep sequence models (a TCN
and a GRU), each trained under two data conditions --- \texttt{real\_only}
and \texttt{real\_plus\_sim} --- to quantify what the dataset's simulated
instances actually add over sparse real positives. Self-supervised
pretraining was defined as a stretch goal conditional on that comparison
being complete, and was not attempted within the project timeframe; the
decision is recorded in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows.
Section~\ref{sec:dataset} characterises the data with measured numbers and
derives the windowing, channel selection and normalisation decisions from
them. Section~\ref{sec:related_work} reviews related work.
Section~\ref{sec:method} describes the baseline features, the two
architectures and the evaluation protocol.
Section~\ref{sec:experimental_setup} gives the grouped cross-validation
design. Section~\ref{sec:results} reports the results and
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} states what 14 events can and cannot support.

\section{Dataset}
\label{sec:dataset}

% Written by M1. Every number below is measured, not quoted from the
% dataset documentation, and is reproducible by:
%   python -m src.data.inventory --root data/3W/dataset --event 9
%   python -m tools.m1_dataset_figures --root data/3W/dataset
%   python -m tools.m1_sensitivity_sweep --root data/3W/dataset
% Sources: DATA_FINDINGS.md, results/variable_availability.csv,
% results/channel_tradeoff.csv, results/m1_sensitivity_sweep.csv.

We use Petrobras's 3W Dataset~2.0.0, event~9 (``Hydrate in Production
Line''), released under CC~BY~4.0. The event-9 folder contains 57 real
instances, 150 simulated instances and 594 Normal-operation instances;
we verified these counts against the dataset's own documentation rather
than assuming them. Each instance is a full-duration, 1\,Hz multivariate
recording of one well, annotated per timestep with a severity class.

\subsection{Instance length}
Measured over the 57 real event-9 instances, an instance runs
\textbf{32{,}135} timesteps at the median (min 7{,}144, max 192{,}581);
55 of 57 individually exceed 10{,}000 timesteps. Simulated instances are
longer and far more uniform (median 45{,}599, all 150 above 10{,}000), and
Normal-operation instances have the widest spread (median 21{,}474, min
10{,}610, max 143{,}231). The median real length is what justifies treating
each instance as a sequence long enough to draw many windows from, and it is
the figure the windowing floor in Section~\ref{sec:dataset_windowing} is set
against.

\subsection{The positive class is rare}
\label{sec:dataset_rare}
Of the 57 real event-9 instances, only \textbf{14} ever contain a
transient-phase label and only \textbf{3} ever reach the established-blockage
label; the remaining 43 contain only normal and unlabelled observations.
This single fact drives the paper's headline metric. The project statement
defines lead time against blockage onset, but an $n=3$ quantity is undefined
on most well-grouped test folds (Section~\ref{sec:setup_nfolds}), so we take
\texttt{failure\_time} to be the annotated \emph{transient} onset --- 14
events across 7 wells --- and cache the blockage onset alongside it so the
original definition can still be reported as a secondary row with its $n$
stated.

Fig.~\ref{fig:transient_duration} shows the distribution of transient-phase
durations over those 14 events: median 3.4\,h, from 3\,min to 13.7\,h. The
30-minute window the models see is marked for scale, and the comparison is
the reason the window span was changed from the 60\,s originally planned
(Section~\ref{sec:dataset_windowing}).
Fig.~\ref{fig:annotated_trace} shows one full instance with its Normal,
Transient and Established zones shaded; the pressure ramp in
\texttt{P-JUS-CKGL} and \texttt{P-ANULAR} and the temperature rise in
\texttt{T-TPT} are visible well before the blockage is annotated, which is
the signal the models are asked to find.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{transient_duration_hist.png}
    \caption{Transient-phase duration for the 14 real event-9 instances that
    reach a transient phase (median 3.4\,h). The models observe a 30-minute
    window, marked for scale.}
    \label{fig:transient_duration}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{annotated_trace.png}
    \caption{One real event-9 instance (\texttt{WELL-00042\_20141218051903})
    with its Normal, Transient and Established zones shaded. The pressure and
    temperature signatures precede the annotated blockage.}
    \label{fig:annotated_trace}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Label monotonicity and unlabelled spans}
\texttt{is\_monotonic\_severity()}, run over every real event-9 instance,
returns \textbf{True for 57/57}: no instance's severity ever reverts from
Established to Transient, or from Transient to Normal. This is a decidable
property of the data rather than a modelling assumption, and it settles a
design question at no cost. Labelling a window by the most severe state it
contains and labelling it by its final timestep are mathematically identical
whenever severity is non-decreasing, so the choice between the two cannot
change any result here; the sweep in Section~\ref{sec:dataset_sensitivity}
confirms this empirically as well.

Every one of the 57 real instances also carries unlabelled (NaN) spans in the
raw class column --- a median of 11.2\,\% of samples, up to 50.4\,\% in the
worst instance. The project statement defines no policy for them. We drop any
window whose label span touches an unlabelled sample, on the conservative
reading that an unlabelled span is not evidence of normal operation: counting
it as Normal would pad the false-alarm denominator with time nobody vouched
for. Section~\ref{sec:dataset_sensitivity} prices that choice exactly.

\subsection{Sensor availability: missing and frozen are different failures}
\label{sec:dataset_availability}
Table~\ref{tab:availability} reports both failure modes per variable over the
57 real instances, length-weighted. A frozen run --- at least 60 identical
consecutive 1\,Hz readings --- is counted separately from a NaN, because a
stuck sensor is not a gap: it reports a plausible number that no imputation
routine flags. The two are disjoint by construction, since a NaN breaks a run
rather than extending it, so they sum to an effective unavailability.

\begin{table}[t]
    \centering

    length-weighted. ``Frozen'' is a run of $\geq 60$ identical consecutive
    readings. Channels are kept when effective unavailability is below
    50\,\%.}
    \label{tab:availability}
    \footnotesize
    \begin{tabular}{lrrrc}
        \toprule
        Variable & Missing\,\% & Frozen\,\% & Effective\,\% & Kept \\
        \midrule
        \texttt{P-MON-CKP}  & 0.0  & 1.1  & 1.1  & yes \\
        \texttt{P-JUS-CKGL} & 0.0  & 2.3  & 2.3  & yes \\
        \texttt{QGL}        & 8.5  & 0.4  & 9.0  & yes \\
        \texttt{T-TPT}      & 26.1 & 10.1 & 36.2 & yes \\
        \texttt{T-JUS-CKP}  & 34.6 & 5.2  & 39.9 & yes \\
        \texttt{P-ANULAR}   & 43.1 & 1.2  & 44.3 & yes \\
        \texttt{P-TPT}      & 15.0 & 35.0 & 50.0 & yes$^{\dagger}$ \\
        \texttt{ABER-CKP}   & 34.9 & 59.6 & 94.6 & no \\

\end{table}

Two observations carry into the rest of the paper. First, \texttt{P-TPT}
clears the 50\,\% cut-off by 0.003\,\%: it is retained or discarded
essentially by rounding, and 70\,\% of its unavailability is frozen rather
than missing. It is also exactly the channel that is dead through three
entire instances, one of which is one of the three blockage events. A
criterion this close to a coin flip is not a channel-selection method, which
is why the channel set is chosen by event coverage instead
(Section~\ref{sec:dataset_channels}). Second, the discrete valve-state
channels (\texttt{ESTADO-*}) are 100\,\% unavailable, split between missing
and frozen: their presence in the schema is not presence in the data.

\subsection{Choosing channels by event coverage}
\label{sec:dataset_channels}
Different wells instrument different sensors, and some sensors are frozen for
the entire duration of specific instances. Selecting channels by \emph{well}
coverage therefore measures the wrong thing. The criterion that matters is
\emph{event} coverage, because an event lost to channel selection cannot be
recovered downstream by any model, whereas lost Normal hours only cost
calibration precision. Table~\ref{tab:channel_tradeoff} gives the trade-off
measured on the built caches --- these are the counts the models actually
train on, not estimates.

\begin{table}[t]
    \centering
    \caption{Channel-set trade-off, measured on the built caches. The
    physically intuitive two-channel set loses 4 of 14 transient events and
    one of the three blockage events.}
    \label{tab:channel_tradeoff}
    \footnotesize
    \begin{tabular}{lccccr}
        \toprule
        Channel set & Ch. & Trans. & Block. & Wells & Normal h \\
        \midrule
        Primary$^{\ddagger}$ & 5 & \textbf{14/14} & \textbf{3/3} & \textbf{7/7} & 1{,}937.7 \\
        \texttt{P-TPT}, \texttt{T-TPT} & 2 & 10/14 & 2/3 & 5/7 & 2{,}885.7 \\
        \bottomrule
    \end{tabular}

    \footnotesize $^{\ddagger}$ \texttt{P-MON-CKP}, \texttt{P-JUS-CKGL},
    \texttt{T-TPT}, \texttt{T-JUS-CKP}, \texttt{P-ANULAR}.
\end{table}

The primary five-channel set is used for every result in this paper. Its
1{,}937.7 Normal hours are 19$\times$ the calibration budget of one alarm per
100\,h, which is ample, while the two-channel alternative buys 948 further
Normal hours --- it retains WELL-00002, the single largest Normal-operation
well --- at the cost of 4 of 14 transient events, 1 of 3 blockages and 2 of 7
positive wells. That set is carried forward only as a sensitivity arm. The
channel list is fitted once over all instances and frozen in the cache
sidecar; Section~\ref{sec:setup_channels} verifies that refitting it per fold
selects the same channels, so the global fit carries no fold information.

\subsection{Disjoint well populations}
\label{sec:dataset_disjoint}
The 15 wells contributing event-9 recordings and the 9 wells contributing
Normal-operation recordings share no well: hydrate wells $\cap$ normal wells
$= \emptyset$. Well identity is consequently a perfect predictor of the
label, and it is recoverable from the signals themselves through baseline
pressures, sensor offsets and calibration differences. We close this shortcut
from two directions. Every signal is normalised \emph{per instance} using
that instance's own statistics, so absolute well-specific levels are removed
before any model sees them --- a correctness requirement here, not a cosmetic
preprocessing step. Section~\ref{sec:setup_grouping} closes it from the other
side by grouping every split by well. Each simulated instance is additionally
treated as its own pseudo-well, which is what makes it possible to exclude
simulated data from validation and test by construction rather than by a
downstream filter.

\subsection{Windowing}
\label{sec:dataset_windowing}
Real transients run for hours (Section~\ref{sec:dataset_rare}), so a window
must span a comparable timescale to contain any of the onset. We decimate the
1\,Hz signal by a factor of 30 --- one sample per 30\,s, the mean of that
block's observed samples --- and keep a window of 60 samples. A window
therefore covers \textbf{30 minutes} while the tensor width stays at 60,
which keeps the TCN's receptive field of 61 sufficient to see the whole
window (Section~\ref{sec:method_arch}). The originally planned 60-second
window would have shown a model roughly 0.5\,\% of a median transient.
Windows are labelled Normal, Transient or Established by the most severe
state present anywhere in the window, which by the monotonicity result above
is equivalent to labelling by the final timestep. Tensors are channels-first,
$[N, C, W]$, and every window carries a binary observation mask so that
imputed and observed samples remain distinguishable downstream.

The resulting cache holds 801 instances and 86{,}088 windows, with 48{,}882
windows dropped by the unlabelled-span and minimum-valid-fraction rules. Of
the windows kept, 42{,}259 come from real instances (1{,}295 Transient, 118
Established --- a real positive rate of 3.34\,\%) and 43{,}829 from simulated
instances (18{,}422 Transient, 21{,}139 Established). The simulated portion
is thus 90.3\,\% positive against a real rate of 3.34\,\%, an imbalance
inversion that Section~\ref{sec:discussion} returns to when interpreting the
\texttt{real\_plus\_sim} condition.

\subsection{Sensitivity of the cache to its discretionary choices}
\label{sec:dataset_sensitivity}
Three choices above are ours rather than the dataset's: the window labelling
rule, the channel set and the unlabelled-span policy. We swept each one at a
time around the primary configuration. Window counts are dominated by the 150
simulated instances, which contain all three phases in nearly every instance
and therefore hide what a configuration change costs on real data, so
Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity} reports real-data event coverage alongside them.

\begin{table}[t]
    \centering
    \caption{One-factor-at-a-time sweeps around the primary cache
    configuration. Window totals are dominated by simulated instances; the
    columns that decide anything are the real-data event counts.}
    \label{tab:sensitivity}
    \footnotesize
    \begin{tabular}{lrrccc}
        \toprule
        Arm & Kept & Dropped & Trans. & Block. & Wells \\
        \midrule
        Primary & 86{,}088 & 48{,}882 & 14 & 3 & 7 \\
        \texttt{final\_timestep} & 86{,}088 & 48{,}882 & 14 & 3 & 7 \\
        \texttt{majority} & 86{,}088 & 48{,}882 & \textbf{12} & \textbf{2} & \textbf{6} \\
        \texttt{P-TPT},\,\texttt{T-TPT} & 98{,}315 & 36{,}655 & 10 & 2 & 5 \\
        NaN $\rightarrow$ Normal & 94{,}498 & 40{,}472 & 14 & 3 & 7 \\
        \bottomrule
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Two of the three results were not predicted. First, \texttt{most\_severe} and
\texttt{final\_timestep} are identical in every column, confirming the
monotonicity result empirically: the choice between the default rule and the
standard alternative cannot change any number in this paper. Second,
\texttt{majority} labelling is \emph{not} label-neutral --- it erases whole
events. It keeps exactly the same number of windows but loses 2 of the 14
transient events, 1 of the 3 blockages and 1 positive well, because an event
whose transient phase never occupies more than half of any 30-minute window
is relabelled Normal everywhere and leaves the positive class entirely. For
rare, slow-onset events that is a concrete argument against majority
labelling rather than a preference. Third, the conservative unlabelled-span
policy costs windows but no events: counting unlabelled spans as Normal adds
8{,}410 windows (+9.8\,\%) and leaves event coverage identical at 14/3/7, so
the price of the conservative choice is statistical power alone.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

% ---- IV-A. Feature Engineering (M3) ----
\subsection{Baseline Feature Engineering}
\label{sec:method_features}


The baseline is treated as a real competitor rather than a formality: it
receives the same folds, the same class-imbalance treatment and the same
calibration step as the deep models, and a recorded tuning budget. A
baseline that was never tuned would make the deep-model comparison
uninterpretable.

\subsubsection{Input}
The baseline consumes the same cache as the deep models: channels-first
\texttt{float32} $[N, C, W]$ windows with an aligned \texttt{uint8} presence
mask, where $\mathrm{mask}=1$ marks a genuinely observed sample. With the
main-arm channel set, $C=5$ and $W=60$ decimated samples at one sample per
30\,s, so each window spans \textbf{30 minutes} with a stride of 150\,s. On
the built cache this gives \textbf{42{,}259 real windows} from 364 usable
real instances, of which 1{,}295 are Transient and 118 Established --- a
positive rate of \textbf{3.34\%}. All 14 transient events and all 3 blockage
events survive the channel choice.

\subsubsection{Multi-timescale, mask-aware features}
For each window and channel we take three nested slices measured
\emph{from the end} of the window (the full 60 samples, the last 30, and the
last 15) and compute six statistics on each: mean, standard deviation,
minimum, maximum, least-squares slope, and the net change between the first
and last present sample. Taking slices from the end is what keeps the
features causal: a spike early in the window can only affect the full-window
statistics, which is verified by a unit test rather than assumed. Every
statistic is computed over \textbf{present samples only}, and the
per-channel presence fraction over the full window is appended as its own
feature block, so the model is told how much of each channel it is trusting.
With $C=5$ this yields $5 \times 6 \times 3 + 5 = 95$ features.

The extractor has no fitted state: every column is a function of one window
and its own mask, with no statistic pooled across rows. Extracting once for
the whole cache is therefore bit-identical to extracting per fold, and the
runner asserts the absence of a \texttt{fit()} at start-up so the property
cannot silently lapse.

\subsubsection{Encoding a dead sensor}
Three real instances carry sensors frozen for their entire recording, and one
of them is a blockage event, so this is not a corner case. When a channel
observes nothing, its statistics are undefined. Emitting $0.0$ is actively
wrong here: per-instance normalisation centres each recording near zero, so
$0.0$ is precisely the value a \emph{healthy} sensor at its own baseline
reports, and that encoding would state that a dead sensor looks normal. We
emit \texttt{NaN} and let XGBoost learn a default branch direction at each
split. The presence fraction remains a real measurement of exactly $0.0$ and
is never \texttt{NaN}. Similarly, the slope is regressed on each sample's
true position inside the slice rather than on its rank among present
samples, so a gap keeps its width and the slope remains a rate; regressing
on rank reports $9.0$ for two points nine steps apart rising nine units.
Section~\ref{sec:results_xgb} reports that neither change is separable from
fold noise on this cache, and we retain both on correctness grounds while
saying so explicitly.

\subsubsection{Class imbalance}
Imbalance is handled with inverse-frequency \texttt{sample\_weight} computed
from each training fold's own class counts. It is deliberately \emph{not}
handled with \texttt{scale\_pos\_weight}, which is a binary-classification
parameter in XGBoost and has no defined effect under
\texttt{multi:softprob} with \texttt{num\_class=3}. \texttt{num\_class=3} is
set explicitly rather than inferred, because a training fold can legitimately
contain no Established windows --- only 118 exist in the entire real cache
--- and the positive-score reduction indexes the third column.

\subsubsection{Tuning and calibration}
Hyperparameters are searched on the \textbf{training fold only}, scored by
grouped inner cross-validation over that fold's wells, across a 16-point
grid. Both conditions of a fold share the configuration selected on that
fold's real training wells, so \texttt{real\_only} and
\texttt{real\_plus\_sim} differ only in training data and not also in
hyperparameters. The scored quantity is validation PR-AUC on
$P(\mathrm{Transient}) + P(\mathrm{Established})$ --- the same reduction the
alarm logic consumes --- and sample weights are applied inside the search
exactly as at final fit time.

Because Module~8 selects the alarm threshold by sweeping a probability axis,
the probabilities must mean what they say. Weighted training on a 3\%
positive rate pushes scores away from the base rate by construction, so
miscalibration is expected rather than incidental. A Platt calibrator is fit
on the \textbf{validation} fold and applied \textbf{unchanged} to that fold's
test wells; Platt is preferred over isotonic because a validation fold holds
only a handful of positive events, where a non-parametric fit would track
noise.

% ---- IV-C. Evaluation Protocol (M5) ----
\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
\label{sec:method_eval}

We evaluate all models using three complementary metrics at a matched
operating point:

\textbf{Lead Time.} For each hydrate event instance, lead time is defined as
the difference between the annotated transient onset time and the first alarm
onset that occurs before it:
\begin{equation}
    \text{lead\_time} = t_{\text{transient\_onset}} - t_{\text{first\_alarm}}
\end{equation}
Following the data analysis in Section~\ref{sec:dataset}, we use the
\emph{transient} onset (label code 109 in the 3W convention) rather than the
blockage onset, because only 3 of 57 real instances reach blockage. The
transient onset is available for all 14 positive-event instances across 7
wells.

\textbf{Event Recall.} The fraction of real hydrate events for which at least
one alarm onset occurs before the transient onset. A missed event (no alarm
before failure) contributes 0; a detected event contributes 1 regardless of
how many alarms fired.

\textbf{False Alarm Rate (FAR).} The number of alarm \emph{onsets} on
Normal-operation instances, divided by the total Normal operating hours in that
fold's test set:
\begin{equation}
    \text{FAR} = \frac{N_{\text{false\_alarm\_onsets}}}{\text{total\_normal\_hours}}
\end{equation}
Critically, we count alarm onsets, not individual windows above threshold —
one sustained false alarm counts as one event, not thousands
(Section~\ref{sec:method_eval}, pitfall W4.1).

\textbf{Operating Point.} All models are compared at a matched target FAR of
$1/100$ per operating hour. The threshold achieving this FAR is selected on
the \emph{validation} fold only (per-fold, per-model), then applied unchanged
to the test fold. This ``freeze'' protocol (S3 in our timeline) ensures that
test-set numbers are never used to tune any hyperparameter.

\textbf{Alarm Definition.} A positive-class probability $p(t)$ is first
smoothed with a causal (trailing) rolling mean of configurable window size.
An alarm fires when the smoothed probability stays above the selected
threshold for at least \texttt{min\_duration} continuous seconds. The causal
smoothing constraint is critical: a centered moving average would leak future
information into the current alarm decision, inflating lead time measurements
(see \texttt{tests/test\_alarm.py} for the regression test guarding this).

\textbf{Supplementary Metrics.} PR-AUC (area under the precision--recall
curve for the collapsed binary positive score), per-class PR-AUC
(Normal/Transient/Established one-vs-rest), and Expected Calibration Error
(ECE) are reported for completeness.


% ====================================================================
% V. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP — M2 writes
% ====================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:experimental_setup}

% Written by M2. Every number below comes from results/fold_report.csv,
% regenerated by:
%   python -m src.data.splits --cache data/cache --n-splits 3 \
%       --n-repeats 1 --val-mode nested \
%       --latex report/tables/fold_report.tex

\subsection{Why grouping by well is not optional here}
\label{sec:setup_grouping}
The two well populations in this dataset are disjoint: the 15 wells
contributing Event-9 recordings and the 9 wells contributing
Normal-Operation recordings share no well. Well identity is therefore a
perfect predictor of the label, and it is recoverable from the signals
themselves --- baseline pressures, sensor offsets and calibration differ
per well. A row-level or instance-level split would let a model reach a high
score by recognising which well it is looking at, and that score would not
survive contact with a new well. Grouping every split by well is what makes
the reported numbers mean what they appear to mean; per-instance
normalisation (Section~\ref{sec:dataset}) closes the same shortcut
from the other side.

\subsection{Two independent splits, paired fold by fold}
A single \texttt{StratifiedGroupKFold} over the union of both populations
does not solve this. Stratifying on the window label cannot control what a
fold receives from each population, so fold composition is left to chance:
one fold can draw five Normal wells and another one. That matters because
Normal hours are the denominator of the false-alarm rate and they are
distributed very unevenly --- WELL-00002 alone holds 1{,}220\,h and
WELL-00007 holds 6\,h. An unlucky draw yields a test fold with tens of
Normal hours, on which a budget of one alarm per 100\,h is not measurable at
all.

We therefore run two independent grouped splits and pair them fold by fold.
Wells carrying at least one positive window are partitioned with the
positive \emph{event} count as the balancing weight; wells carrying none are
partitioned with their Normal \emph{hours} as the weight. Both use
longest-processing-time-first greedy assignment --- the heaviest remaining
well goes to the lightest fold --- with ties broken at random within a
10\,\% tolerance of the lightest load. Test fold $i$ is the union of part
$i$ of each partition. Without event weighting, WELL-00042 alone (5 of the
14 transient instances) would dominate whichever fold received it.

\subsection{Nested validation}
\label{sec:setup_validation}
Each fold yields a nested \texttt{(train, val, test)} split, with validation
drawn only from that fold's training wells. Validation serves two purposes
that need different things, so its wells are chosen two different ways.
Early stopping and hyperparameter selection need positive events, so
positive wells enter validation as one event-balanced slice of the training
pool. Threshold selection (Section~\ref{sec:method_eval}) needs Normal
\emph{hours}, because it tunes an operating point against a rate of one
alarm per 100\,h; a proportional slice does not guarantee them --- an
earlier proportional design left one fold with 4.0 validation hours --- so
Normal wells are added smallest-first until 300\,h is reached, and no
further. The floor is a measurement requirement, not a tuning choice: below
it the validation false-alarm rate cannot resolve the target.

\subsection{Number of folds}
\label{sec:setup_nfolds}
Seven wells carry a positive window, which bounds the fold count from above.
We use $k=3$ with a single repeat. Table~\ref{tab:folds} is the fold report
that decided it, and it is generated before any model is trained.

\input{tables/fold_report.tex}

The alternative we measured was leave-one-well-out over the seven positive
wells. It fails on the false-alarm denominator: five of its seven test folds
fall below 300 Normal hours, with the thinnest at 49.9\,h --- half the
window needed to observe a single alarm at the target rate. Its positive
side is no better balanced, ranging from one to five events per test fold.
At $k=3$ every test fold instead holds 4--5 positive events and 509--562
Normal hours. That is the reason for the choice, and it was made from
Table~\ref{tab:folds} rather than from any model's score.

The choice is not free, and the cost falls on the training side.
Leave-one-well-out would leave five positive wells in every training fold;
$k=3$ leaves 5, 2 and 4 (Table~\ref{tab:folds}). Fold~1's two wells are
what makes its grouped inner cross-validation unable to produce a split
with positives on both sides, so hyperparameter search falls back to
defaults for that fold (Section~\ref{sec:results_baserate}). We accepted a
badly conditioned \emph{training} fold in exchange for test folds on which
the headline false-alarm rate is measurable at all, because a
hyperparameter search that degrades to a default configuration still
yields a usable model, whereas a test fold with 49.9 Normal hours cannot
evaluate one. With 7 positive wells no split avoids both.

Three folds are few, and we do not claim otherwise. With one repeat, the
reported spread is the spread over three fold compositions; the variance
this leaves is quantified in Section~\ref{sec:results_baserate} and revisited
in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

\subsection{Simulated data and the freeze}
Simulated instances are excluded from the validation and test candidate
pools entirely, by construction rather than by a downstream filter: each
simulated instance is its own pseudo-well (Section~\ref{sec:dataset}) and
those pseudo-wells are never eligible for either side. They enter
\texttt{train\_idx} only under the \texttt{real\_plus\_sim} condition; the
\texttt{real\_only} condition drops them. This is the only difference
between the two conditions of Result~1 --- the folds themselves are
identical, so the comparison is paired on wells.

\subsection{The one exception to training-fold-only fitting, measured}
\label{sec:setup_channels}
The cache is built once, before the folds exist, so its channel list is
selected over every instance rather than per fold. This is the single
documented departure from "fit the variable selector on the training fold
only", and it is only harmless if the same wells would have been selected
inside each fold. We measured that rather than asserting it
(\texttt{tools/m2\_channel\_constancy.py}): refitting the missingness
criterion on each fold's training wells alone keeps the \emph{same} seven
channels in all three folds. The list does not move with the folds, so the
global fit carried no information about which wells a fold holds out.

The shipped cache uses five channels rather than those seven, because the
channel set was pinned for event coverage (Section~\ref{sec:dataset})
rather than by the missingness threshold --- the threshold route would add
\texttt{P-PDG}, \texttt{P-TPT} and \texttt{QGL} and drop
\texttt{P-ANULAR}. That is a difference of criteria, chosen and documented
before any model was trained; what the measurement above establishes is
the separate, leakage-relevant claim that neither route depends on the
fold.

\subsection{Freezing}
The split configuration --- $k=3$, one repeat, nested validation, seed
42 --- was frozen before test evaluation and has not been revised since.
The fold design was not changed after any test number was seen, including
where a test number suggested it should be (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

% ---- VI-A. XGBoost Baseline Results (M3) ----
\subsection{XGBoost Baseline}
\label{sec:results_xgb}


\subsubsection{Validation performance}
Table~\ref{tab:xgb_folds} gives validation PR-AUC over the three grouped
folds at a positive-window base rate of $0.0334$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{XGBoost validation PR-AUC per fold (seed 42). The standard
deviation exceeds the mean; see Section~\ref{sec:results_xgb} for why.}
\label{tab:xgb_folds}
\begin{tabular}{cccc}
\toprule
Fold & Positive val.\ events & \texttt{real\_only} & \texttt{real\_plus\_sim} \\
\midrule
0 & 1 & 0.0005 & 0.0003 \\
1 & 3 & \textbf{0.7755} & 0.2420 \\
2 & 5 & 0.0751 & 0.1288 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{c}{mean $\pm$ sd} & $0.284 \pm 0.428$ & $0.124 \pm 0.121$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Simulated data did not help. The paired difference
(\texttt{real\_plus\_sim} $-$ \texttt{real\_only}) is $-0.160 \pm 0.325$,
negative in two of three folds. This is a distribution argument rather than
a sample-size one: the simulated windows are \textbf{90.3\%} positive
(39{,}561 of 43{,}829) against a \textbf{3.34\%} real positive rate, and they
inflate the training set from roughly 19k to 63k rows, pulling the model
toward a regime that does not exist in the real wells it is scored on.
\texttt{real\_only} is therefore the headline condition.

\subsubsection{PR-AUC is not comparable across these folds}
\label{sec:results_baserate}
Each fold's validation split has a different positive base rate, and PR-AUC
rises mechanically with it. Fold~0's validation set contains \textbf{exactly
one positive window} out of 11{,}260 (base rate $10^{-4}$), fold~1 has 463
of 7{,}327 ($0.0632$) and fold~2 has 638 of 11{,}592 ($0.0550$) --- more
than two orders of magnitude apart. A PR-AUC computed from a single positive
row is that row's reciprocal rank, not a performance estimate. Read as lift
over each fold's own base rate, the baseline is above chance in all three
folds ($1.4\times$, $12.3\times$, $3.5\times$) rather than at chance in two
of them, which is what the raw column suggests.

This is not a pedantic point, and we report it because the uncorrected
analysis is the natural one to run and it misleads. On raw PR-AUC the number
of positive validation events correlates strongly with score across the
ablation's 18 cells (Spearman $\rho = 0.638$, $p = 0.0044$), which invites
the conclusion that sparse folds cannot measure anything. That correlation
\textbf{does not survive base-rate correction}: on lift, $\rho = -0.14$
($p = 0.58$). Folds with more positive events also have higher base rates.
The same trap applies to any per-fold PR-AUC comparison in this project,
including the head-to-head model table.

\subsubsection{Fold composition dominates every other source of variance}
The feature ablation ran 9 extractor variants over 18 paired cells (3 CV
split seeds $\times$ 3 folds $\times$ 2 model seeds) on validation folds
only. Decomposing the variance across those 162 runs on the
base-rate-corrected scale, the variance of the feature-design arm means is
$2.09\times10^{-2}$ while the variance of the fold-cell means is $0.988$:
fold composition accounts for roughly \textbf{47$\times$} more spread than
the entire feature-design space we searched. (On the raw scale the ratio is
$448\times$, but part of that is the base-rate artifact above rather than
genuine instability.) Anything selected on validation PR-AUC in a
single-positive-window fold --- including the deep models' early stopping
and Module~8's threshold selection --- is selected on noise.

One training fold could not be tuned at all: in fold~1 every positive window
in the training split belongs to a \emph{single} well, so grouped inner
cross-validation cannot produce a split with positives on both sides. All
three inner splits were unusable and that fold fell back to the default
configuration. With 7 positive wells and 3 outer folds this is a structural
property of the dataset, not an accident of one seed.

\subsubsection{Feature-design ablation: null results}
Arms were compared as paired differences on identical folds and seeds and
tested with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, restricted to the 10 cells where
validation PR-AUC is estimable, and expressed as base-rate-corrected lift
ratios per Section~\ref{sec:results_baserate}. The presence-fraction block
is worth $1.175\times$ (7/10 wins, $p = 0.027$); one timescale versus three
$1.027\times$ ($p = 0.92$); \texttt{NaN} versus $0.0$ encoding of a dead
sensor $1.025\times$ ($p = 0.77$); the slope's time axis $0.977\times$
($p = 0.63$); two timescales versus three $0.914\times$ ($p = 0.23$).

Only the presence-fraction block separates from noise, and it does so on
both the raw and corrected scales; everything else is within 3\% of parity.
Even that result would not survive a Bonferroni correction for the six
comparisons made ($p < 0.0083$), so we read it as suggestive --- but it is the only arm
where direction, win count and $p$-value agree, and
Section~\ref{sec:results_shortcut} supplies an independent mechanism for
why. We retain the two changed defaults on correctness grounds --- $0.0$ is
the value a healthy sensor at its own baseline reports, and a slope
regressed on sample rank is not a rate --- rather than claiming the numbers
supported them. Three timescales are kept because the module contract
specifies them; one timescale (35 features instead of 95) performs the same
within noise.

\subsubsection{The baseline partly reads instrumentation, not physics}
\label{sec:results_shortcut}
Gain importance on fold~1, the only fold with substantial validation signal,
placed \textbf{40.8\% of the total gain on the 5 presence-fraction columns}
out of 95. We tested the implication directly by training on those columns
\emph{only}, with no sensor values of any kind, over 9 fold-cells. The
presence-only model reaches a mean validation PR-AUC of \textbf{0.172}
against \textbf{0.233} for the full 95-feature model --- \textbf{74\% of the
full performance without seeing a single pressure or temperature reading}
--- and in 2 of 9 cells it \emph{outperforms} all 90 value features (0.493
versus 0.354, and 0.284 versus 0.259).

The explanation is in the dataset. Missingness here is well-specific:
different wells instrument different sensors, and some sensors are dead for
an entire instance. Because the hydrate wells and the Normal-operation wells
are disjoint populations, sensor availability is a proxy for well identity,
and well identity is very nearly the label. Per-instance normalisation, the
project's main defence against well-identity confounding, removes each
recording's offset and scale but cannot remove \emph{``this channel is
absent''}, which lives in the mask rather than in the values.

Consistently with this, permutation importance neither reproduces the
expected physical signature nor reproduces itself across folds: pairwise
rank agreement is nil (Kendall $\tau = +0.20, +0.40, -0.40$; all
$p > 0.48$). In fold~1 the top-ranked channel is \texttt{P-ANULAR}, the
annulus, which does not communicate with the service line, while
\texttt{P-MON-CKP} --- the pressure upstream of the production choke, which
the restriction mechanism predicts should dominate --- ranks last with a
mean share of $0.002$. \textbf{We therefore do not claim that the baseline
recovered the physical hydrate signature.} Claiming otherwise would have
required quoting one fold and ignoring the other two.

\subsubsection{Calibration}
Calibration behaved as intended in every fold and both conditions. Platt
scaling fit on validation reduced expected calibration error from $0.0409$
to $0.0106$ under \texttt{real\_only} and from $0.0538$ to $0.0121$ under
\texttt{real\_plus\_sim} (a 74--78\% reduction), and the Brier score by 29\%
in both, improving in all 6 fold~$\times$~condition cells. Because Module~8
selects the alarm threshold by sweeping a probability axis, this is a
prerequisite for that threshold to transfer, not a cosmetic step.
Fig.~\ref{fig:reliability} shows the before/after curves with a per-bin count
panel beneath; at a 3\% positive rate the high-probability bins hold very few
windows, and a reliability curve that hides bin populations makes a handful
of unlucky windows look like systematic miscalibration.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{reliability_xgboost.png}
\caption{Reliability of the XGBoost baseline on a validation fold, before
and after Platt scaling. Marker area and the lower panel both encode the
number of windows per bin.}
\label{fig:reliability}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Tuning budget}
The search evaluated the full 16-configuration grid per fold under grouped
inner CV, and both conditions of a fold share the configuration selected on
that fold's real training wells, so the two conditions differ only in
training data. Selected configurations were consistent
(\texttt{max\_depth}~$=3$, \texttt{n\_estimators}~$=300$ in both tunable
folds): the search preferred the smallest and shallowest models offered,
the expected outcome with roughly 1{,}400 positive windows.

% ====================================================================
% VII. DISCUSSION & LIMITATIONS — M2 writes
% ====================================================================
\section{Discussion and Limitations}
\label{sec:discussion}

% Written by M2. Numbers are from results/summary.csv,
% results/fold_report.csv and results/window_sensitivity_validation_summary.csv.

\subsection{What 14 events can and cannot support}
The real Event-9 subset contains 57 instances, of which \textbf{14} reach a
transient phase and \textbf{3} reach established blockage, spread over 7 and
3 wells respectively. Every claim in this paper rests on those 14 events,
and the fold structure divides them 5/5/4 across test folds
(Table~\ref{tab:folds}).

This supports statements about whether a method detects anything at all at a
fixed false-alarm budget. It does not support ranking the three models
against each other. In every cell of the head-to-head comparison the
standard deviation across folds is comparable to or larger than the mean ---
event recall for XGBoost under \texttt{real\_only} is $0.23 \pm 0.25$, with
per-fold values of $0.00$, $0.20$ and $0.50$. Section~\ref{sec:results_baserate}
quantifies the same point from the other direction: fold composition
accounts for roughly $47\times$ more spread than the entire feature-design
space searched. A model comparison on three folds of this dataset measures
which wells landed where.

\subsection{The headline metric had to be redefined, and remains weak}
DL8.3 defines lead time against established-blockage onset. That onset
exists in 3 of 57 real instances, so on grouped folds most test sides
contain none and the metric is undefined there. We therefore define
\texttt{failure\_time} as the annotated \emph{transient} onset (14
instances, 7 wells) and report blockage-referenced lead time only as a
secondary quantity with its $n=3$ stated.

Even redefined, lead time is the weakest number in this paper. It is
computed from the events a model actually flags, and across the six
model\,$\times$\,condition cells that is between 0 and 2 events. A median
over two observations is reported for completeness in
Section~\ref{sec:results_comparison}; it should not be read as a performance
estimate, and we do not build any conclusion on it.

\subsection{The operating point does not transfer across wells}
\label{sec:discussion_threshold}
This is the most actionable negative result we obtained. Thresholds are
selected on validation to sit at or below one alarm per 100 operating hours
and then applied frozen to test. On test the realised rate is
\textbf{1.8 to 7.9} alarms per 100\,h across the six cells --- the budget is
exceeded everywhere, by up to a factor of eight.

The failure is not simply that the threshold is too permissive, because
event recall stays low at the same time (0.00--0.23; two cells flag zero of
14 events). A threshold that is simultaneously too low for the false-alarm
budget and too high to catch events means the score distribution on test
wells has shifted relative to validation: the model's alarms land on Normal
data rather than on events. Ranking itself is not the whole story --- five of the six
cells score above the $0.0334$ positive base rate on test PR-AUC, by
$3.4\times$ to $6.3\times$ --- but the absolute score scale on which the
threshold lives does not survive the move to unseen wells.

Table~\ref{tab:folds} shows why this was likely from the start. Every
validation fold contains \textbf{exactly one} positive well. An operating
point is therefore always fitted to a single well's score distribution and
then applied to 1--4 different wells. Given that well identity is close to
the label in this dataset (Section~\ref{sec:results_shortcut}), a
well-specific operating point is what one should expect. A relative
threshold --- a quantile of each well's own Normal-score distribution rather
than an absolute probability --- follows directly from this diagnosis and is
the first thing we would test with more time. We did not test it here,
because the diagnosis came after test evaluation and adopting it now would
be selection on test.

\subsection{One fold cannot validate anything}
Fold~0's validation split contains \textbf{one positive window} out of
11{,}260. Early stopping, calibration and threshold selection are all fitted
on that split, and none of the three is defined at $n=1$: a probability
calibrator cannot be fitted at all, and validation PR-AUC degenerates to the
reciprocal rank of a single row (Section~\ref{sec:results_baserate}).
Fold~1 has a matching pathology on the training side --- all of its training
positives belong to one well, so grouped inner cross-validation has no split
with positives on both sides and hyperparameter search fell back to defaults
for that fold.

Both are consequences of partitioning 7 positive wells into 3 folds, not of
a particular seed. We report them rather than repairing them: the folds were
frozen before test evaluation, and re-cutting them after seeing that fold~0
produced a near-zero score would be exactly the selection this protocol
exists to prevent.

\subsection{Disjoint well populations bound external validity}
The hydrate and Normal-Operation wells share no well, so "generalising to a
new well" and "generalising to a new class of well" cannot be separated in
this data. Grouping by well and per-instance normalisation remove the
offset- and scale-based routes to well identity, but not all of them: the
presence-only ablation in Section~\ref{sec:results_shortcut} reaches 74\,\%
of full-feature validation performance using \emph{no} sensor values,
because which channels exist is itself well-specific. Any deployment claim
would need wells that contribute both Normal and hydrate recordings, which
this release does not provide.

\subsection{Simulated data shifts the problem rather than enlarging it}
Simulated instances are 90.3\,\% positive windows against a 3.34\,\% real
rate, and all 150 of them reach the established-blockage phase that only 3
real instances reach. Adding them triples the training set and moves the
model toward a regime the real test wells do not contain. The measured
effect is mixed and consistent with that reading: for XGBoost it improves
test PR-AUC ($0.11 \rightarrow 0.21$) and the false-alarm rate
($7.9 \rightarrow 1.8$ per 100\,h) while reducing event recall
($0.23 \rightarrow 0.17$). \texttt{real\_only} is the headline condition for
this reason.

\subsection{Known asymmetries and untested choices}
Three limitations are ours rather than the dataset's.

First, the baseline's probabilities are calibrated on validation and the
deep models' are not: \texttt{tools/train\_xgb.py} fits a Platt calibrator
per fold, while \texttt{tools/train\_deep\_models.py} has no calibration
stage. Reported ECE is therefore not a like-for-like comparison, and the
deep models' figures --- TCN reaches a validation ECE of 0.48 uncalibrated
against 0.01 with a calibrator fitted on the same fold --- reflect that gap
rather than a property of the architecture. This does not explain the recall
gap in Section~\ref{sec:discussion_threshold}: a monotone calibrator applied
to validation and test alike leaves every threshold decision unchanged, and
we verified that the ranking is unchanged wherever the fitted calibrator is
monotone.

Second, the window length is not settled. A validation-only sensitivity run
comparing 15-minute against the adopted 30-minute context finds 15 minutes
better on mean validation PR-AUC in 3 of the 4 model\,$\times$\,condition
cells (most sharply for TCN under \texttt{real\_only}, $0.14$ against
$0.04$). The adopted length was chosen from measured transient durations
before any model was trained, and it was not revisited after test
evaluation; we report the sensitivity run as an open question rather than a
correction.

Third, self-supervised pretraining on the large unlabelled segments ---
listed as a stretch goal --- was \textbf{not attempted within the project
timeframe}. No result in this paper should be read as evidence about it.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

\placeholder{M5 fills after S3 FREEZE: [Model X] under the [Condition Y] condition provided the best early warning capability, achieving a median lead time of [Z] minutes at the target false-alarm budget of 1 per 100 hours. The inclusion of simulated data [improved/degraded/had mixed effects on] model performance. The primary limitation of this study remains the small sample size of real transient events (14 instances across 7 wells) and the strict separation of normal and hydrate wells, which makes generalizing to new wells challenging. Future work will investigate self-supervised (SSL) pre-training on the vast unlabeled segments to further improve representation robustness.}
